knowledge.assertion: the prepare-recovery rejection has no repair; the gated restarts are on the proposal-phase handlers
fixed ballot per replica, climbing only with IsLeader; boundary against the peers' stored ballot

counterevidence: The gate is a boundary, not a blanket inability: the owner control and the above-ballot round both show the same instance advancing when the recoverer's ballot exceeds the stored one, so replicas whose fixed ballot is above the stored ballot are unaffected.
The peers' answers are legitimate protocol behaviour: each reports the ballot it stored, and the rejected tries were genuinely below it, so the rejections do not themselves violate a peer duty.

The blocked state requires a stored ballot above the recoverer's fixed ballot; in the receipts it came from a recovery attempt that failed after broadcasting its Prepare, which is a permitted failure but a specific one.

The recoverers that hold the instance without its command cannot substitute another path: their only entry point is startRecoveryForInstance, whose prepare uses makeBallot's fixed ballot; a replica that already holds the value is not blocked in the same way, as the value-adoption control showed.

The conclusion does not depend on where the gated restarts sit: the prepare-recovery path has no repair (epaxos/epaxos.go:1216-1219), and the two restarts that exist belong to the proposal-phase handlers, which a blocked recoverer never reaches because its prepare never completes.
limitations: One configuration (N=5, F=2, instance (0,0)) with the stored ballot fixed at 7; the boundary was exercised at fixed ballots 0, 6 and 8, so an intermediate stored ballot and higher ballot rounds (id+2N and beyond) were not exercised.

The harness invoked startRecoveryForInstance directly instead of waiting for the executor's COMMIT_GRACE_PERIOD retry (epaxos/epaxos.go:404-417) and scheduled all deliveries explicitly, so the retry cadence and transport timing are modelled.

The premise that the accepting peers store the higher ballot was produced by failing replica 2 after its Prepare broadcast; a real deployment could reach the same state through the same permitted failure, which was not exercised end-to-end.

No client or executor existed in these runs, so the blocked replica's consequence for a waiting client is characterised at the protocol level (an uncommitted instance whose dependents cannot execute) rather than measured as a completion interval.
interpretations.joint_history: Indices 0-6, 10, 11, 15-17, 20, 21, 23-28 and 31-35 belong to receipt 911d45335b3047178a6fd739f24b2cfb (owner-recoverer run); indices 8, 12, 14, 17, 19 and 20 belong to receipt c342db60ffff4e42889bf53646049491 (non-owner boundary run, same instance (0,0) and same scenario, corrected alias successor). Each statement names its receipt; no measurement is combined across executions.

interpretations.rationale: Current account: the anomaly is resolved and it is a defect distinct from the fabricated-self-ballot one. Receipt 81a44ff62122417db3cc5697fc5303f6 (fixed experiment 0757162a4aa64ef4a58a90002641eb27-experiment) shows the owner holding its command X at status ACCEPTED before its own recovery (index 0), the empty acceptor at status NONE after the Accept (index 3), and, after the owner recovered its own instance and the three PrepareReplies were delivered, an instance left at status PREACCEPTED with an empty command list plus bookkeeping whose candidate command is an empty slice (index 4: inst_cmds_len 0, inst_status 1, lb_cmds_len 0, lb_status 1, lb_appended 1, lb_nacks 0), with no command proposed afterwards (index 5) and the same values in the second run (indices 9-11); comparison 0 and comparison 1 are both violated with witnesses 5 and 11. The mechanism is now sourced: a reply from a replica that holds no command carries a nil command slice, the decoder allocates it with make([]state.Command, alen1) so the receiver sees a non-nil empty slice (epaxos/defs.go:228-235), the adoption loop copies that empty slice into lb.cmds because its VBallot equals the running candidate ballot (epaxos/epaxos.go:1239-1246), and the sub-case 5/6 fallback substitutes state.NOOP() only when lb.cmds is nil (epaxos/epaxos.go:1307-1311), which an empty slice is not - so startPhase1 is called with an empty command batch and the instance becomes PREACCEPTED with Cmds of length zero (epaxos/epaxos.go:1291-1296, 751-779). That also explains why the probe recorded no PreAccept command (proposed_cmd_op -1 was the empty batch, not an absent proposal) and why the probe's two runs coincided: the empty slice wins in both delivery orders because the loop adopts ties with >= and the empty reply is adopted whatever its position, the last delivery being irrelevant. Consequences for the captured package: the instance is proposed and can be decided with no command at all, replacing the command the owner itself held; executeCommands accepts an empty non-nil batch because its guard is a nil test, so the instance executes as a no-op rather than stalling; and the client re-offer path that protects the fabricated-NOOP case does not fire here, because handleCommit tests for exactly one command with operation NONE (epaxos/epaxos.go:1090-1099), which an empty batch never satisfies. A second receipt measures the client-side consequence of exactly that decision: receipt 098ab4425325464192aa558be557f0ce (fixed experiment 49b316fdc67c459fb374500fb7f26514-experiment) attaches a real client proposal (command id 91) to the owner's own instance, that instance's own recovery decides the empty batch, and both declared comparisons are violated with complete witness 4 - the decided instance holds a command list of length zero while the owner held command X before (index 0: status 3, cmd_op 1) and the owner's pending request is never re-offered (requeued 0 with pending_proposals 1 and reply_bytes 0), while the single-NOOP decision of the same family (receipt 893f6180a4514a8d9e20a1d5e6698542) re-queued its request and later completed it. The contrast is the re-offer guard's own condition: handleCommit requires exactly one command with operation NONE (epaxos/epaxos.go:1090-1099), which an empty batch never satisfies, so the empty-command decision drops the client's request with neither a reply nor a re-offer. The delivery-order question is now measured with three runs of the same reply set (receipt e89ecb076e8d4a78b174f848562ed77f, fixed experiment e8fb81e1cb0742118ce33f60e08a0de1-experiment): with the replies delivered as 2,4,3 the instance ends with no command (comparison 0 violated, witness 6); as 3,4,2 the same outcome (comparison 1 violated, witness 13); and as 3,2,4 - where the command-carrying reply is the second delivered - the instance keeps the owner's command (comparison 2 holds, evaluated 20). The mechanism is therefore not a simple last-reply-wins rule over the whole set but the timing of the quorum trigger: handlePrepareReply dispatches as soon as len(lb.prepareReplies) reaches SlowQuorumSize, which for one self reply and a five-replica configuration is two peer replies, and the candidate command is whatever the last adopted reply in that prefix carries. In this reply set two peers carry no command and one carries X, so two of the three delivery orders put an empty reply in the adopted position and lose the command, while the third order puts X there and keeps it. The adopted value therefore depends on arrival order among equally admissible replies rather than on their content, and the empty-slice handling is what makes the losing orders lose the command outright instead of substituting state.NOOP(). The earlier statement that the order variant was unmeasured is withdrawn; the state/command invariant entry is qualified rather than wrong: it holds for the command-carrying writers, while this path reaches the same status-without-command combination through an empty non-nil slice, which that entry's nil test does not cover. The deciding position is now observed rather than derived, with a four-order receipt on a fixed reply set that holds two command-carrying and two empty peer replies (receipt 251562364ca64b3c80cd14e0d6aeddc3, fixed experiment e25f403842234594881914f730efff4e-experiment, test TestAssuranceEPaxosRecoveryMixedQuorumOrder, exit 0, 40 parsed events, no diagnostics). The harness reads the recoverer's leader-bookkeeping pointer before and after every delivery, so the trigger is observed as the delivery that replaces that object: in all four orders the replacement happens on the second delivered peer reply - index 5 for the order 1,2,3,4 with reply 2 carrying the command, index 15 for 1,3,4,2 with reply 3 carrying none, index 25 for 3,4,1,2 with reply 4 carrying none, index 35 for 3,1,4,2 with reply 1 carrying the command - and the fresh bookkeeping that startPhase1 installs already carries the decision (fresh_lb_ballot -1, fresh_lb_status 1, fresh_lb_cmds_len 1 when the trigger reply carried the command and 0 when it did not). The outcomes then follow that position and nothing else: comparison 0 holds for 1,2,3,4 (index 9: owner_cmds_len 1, proposed_cmd_op 1, trigger reply 2); comparison 1 is violated for 1,3,4,2 with complete witness 19 (owner_cmds_len 0, proposed_cmds_len 0), where the first delivered reply carried X while the trigger reply did not, so a command-carrying reply present when the trigger fires does not protect the command and the empty reply need not arrive first; comparison 2 is violated for 3,4,1,2 with complete witness 29, where both command-carrying replies are delivered after the trigger and the instance stays empty although there are now as many command-carrying as empty peer replies in the set; and comparison 3 holds for 3,1,4,2 (index 39: owner_cmds_len 1, trigger reply 1) although the first delivered reply carried nothing and the empty replies outnumber the command-carrying one in the queue before the trigger. The reply set is fixed across the four runs, so the number of command-carrying replies does not decide the outcome: the trigger prefix holds the recoverer's own reply plus two peer replies, and the owner's command survives exactly when the second peer reply carries it. The three-order tie receipt that left half the permutation space open is now completed (receipt 2ba5ed477d854a01adbca361e9a8a918, fixed experiment 1479f8725fce4b139838cfa202f7a2a1-experiment, test TestAssuranceEPaxosRecoverySameBallotOrder, exit 0, 42 parsed events, no diagnostics): with the same reply set as the earlier tie runs, the orders 2,3,4 and 4,3,2 put an empty reply at the trigger position and lose the command (comparison 0 violated with complete witness 27; comparison 2 violated with complete witness 41), while 4,2,3 puts the command-carrying reply there after an empty first delivery and keeps it (comparison 1 holds, evaluated 34). Together with the three orders of the earlier receipt, all six permutations of this reply set follow the trigger position - 2,4,3, 3,4,2, 2,3,4 and 4,3,2 drop the command, 3,2,4 and 4,2,3 keep it - so the completed permutation space contains no order that contradicts the mechanism. The last axis the question still listed as unmeasured is closed by counting rather than by a new run. After the recovery dispatch, the replies that can still arrive are the peer replies not yet delivered, N - SlowQuorumSize of them, because the recoverer's own reply plus the first SlowQuorumSize - 1 peer replies were consumed by the dispatch; for N=5 that is two replies against a threshold of three, and since N - (N+1)/2 is smaller than (N+1)/2 for every N, no configuration of this path can re-reach the threshold on the fresh bookkeeping. The four-order receipt already measured the first half of that: after the trigger its fresh bookkeeping held no appended replies (lb_appended 0) and then one and two as the two remaining replies landed in it, with no further dispatch and the instance unchanged. So the empty-command adoption is final once the trigger fires, and the remaining discriminator item is answered as structurally impossible rather than unmeasured. The execution side of that decision is pinned to source as well. An instance that is COMMITTED with a non-nil zero-length command list passes every guard on the executor's path: executeCommands leaves it alone rather than routing it to recovery because its status is at least COMMITTED and its Cmds are non-nil (epaxos/epaxos.go:398-404), executeCommand admits it once its status is COMMITTED (epaxos/exec.go:24-30), and strongconnect refuses only a nil slice (epaxos/exec.go:76-78). The loop that applies a batch is bounded by len(w.Cmds) (epaxos/exec.go:122-127), so a zero-length batch applies nothing, writes no reply even where the instance still holds pending proposals, and the instance is nevertheless marked EXECUTED at the end of its SCC block (epaxos/exec.go:132); executeCommands then advances ExecedUpTo over it (epaxos/epaxos.go:398-402 and 421-423), so the instance neither stalls its row nor comes back through recovery, and the instances queued behind it become executable. The client-visible effect therefore has two independent causes: the reply write sits inside the per-command loop, which never runs for a zero-length batch, and the re-offer guard is not satisfied because handleCommit requires exactly one command with operation NONE. The executor anchors used in this account are now registered materials rather than bare line numbers: the executor's admission guard, the nil-slice check in the SCC walk, the batch-application loop and the driver loop that advances ExecedUpTo. The executor ranges registered for this account were checked against the snapshot; the admission guard is now also registered as the exact function bounds (epaxos/exec.go:25-42), while the nil-slice check, the batch-application block and the driver loop were confirmed as they stand. The two neighbouring entries that touch the same path were re-read against this account and need no change: the ballot-gated adoption entry names NOOP substitution only for a nil candidate, which is the branch its own condition describes, and the rejection entry states the nacks-before-append rule and the two IsLeader-gated restarts that the receipts support. The decoding claim was tightened by inspection: the same run-time slice allocation appears in a second decoder of the same file (PreAccept.Unmarshal, epaxos/defs.go:362-366), which is now a registered source. Closing checks on this account: the harness draft is identical to the frozen basis of the last fixed experiment and to its scratch copy, so a future revision starts from the reviewed text; the status-guard account next door rightly carries no experiment binding because its retry receipt belongs to another investigation's experiment. Closing note: with the interval ending, this account's statements, its citations and the source ranges it relies on have all been re-read together and the last checks confirmed the recorded wording rather than changing it.

c60acf998d394127b5cef04b47bcee00-gap-3.explanation: Resolved: the path is sub-case 5/6 of handlePrepareReply together with the sub-case fallback. The owner's bookkeeping ended with an empty candidate command and a single appended reply because the dispatch replaced inst.lb with the fresh bookkeeping that startPhase1 creates (hence ballot -1, status PREACCEPTED and the empty slice it was handed) and one further reply was appended to that new bookkeeping, while the instance fields were overwritten with lb.cmds/lb.status before the dispatch (epaxos/epaxos.go:1291-1296) - which is how the instance reached PREACCEPTED with an empty command list.

e12170eb561b4cdd9d5760b259ca8838-gap-4.explanation: Resolved in favour of the target path: the recorded state came from the package's own handling of an empty (nil-on-the-wire) command slice, not from a startPhase1 call with an empty batch issued by the probe. The probe called startPhase1 once, with the command X, and never with an empty slice; the empty slice appeared only when a reply from a replica holding no command was decoded (epaxos/defs.go:228-235) and adopted into lb.cmds.

counterevidence: The replacement needs a reply that carries no command at a value ballot at least as high as the recovering replica's candidate ballot; in this run that reply came from an acceptor that never pre-accepted, which required the accept broadcast to skip a failed peer, so the same reachability limit as the value-adoption finding applies.

The owner's command is not re-offered by the captured package in this scenario, and that is now measured rather than derived: receipt 098ab4425325464192aa558be557f0ce shows the decided instance holding an empty command list, the pending proposal count at 1 and nothing on the owner's propose channel, so the client-visible completion depends on the client's own retry rather than on the re-offer path that covers the single-NOOP case.

The outcome is order-dependent rather than inevitable: the third recorded order (3,2,4) kept the owner's command with the same reply set, so the empty-command loss is contingent on which reply is adopted last before the quorum trigger, not a property of the replies' content alone.

All recorded runs of the order variant come from one construction and one configuration (the pre-accept wave and the accept wave are both Thrifty subsets, so two peers hold the command and two hold nothing); the four-order receipt repeats that construction rather than reproducing the replacement in an independent scenario.

The measurement is bounded to the owner-as-recoverer case with one pending proposal; it does not show what a client library would do next, since no client process ran and the reply writer stayed empty.

The earlier claim that the two first runs refuted order dependence is withdrawn: those runs did not apply an order at all, and the order receipts show the opposite - the same message set yields two different decided commands depending only on which reply occupies the trigger position.

The loss is still a specific interleaving: it requires an empty reply to be the second delivered peer reply, and the four orders were chosen by the harness rather than sampled from a network, so the runs show that the outcome is fixed by that position and not how often such an interleaving occurs.

The completed permutation space is one reply set in one configuration: the trigger falls on the second delivered peer reply only because the recoverer's own fabricated reply counts toward SlowQuorumSize, and no run varies that quorum or uses a reply set whose value ballots differ.
The counting argument that closes the post-trigger axis is derived from source plus the measured reply accounting, not executed: no run drives a second dispatch, because none can.
The executor reading is a source derivation: the guards and loops cited are the ones a run would take, but no receipt shows an instance with a zero-length batch actually reaching EXECUTED.
limitations: One configuration and instance (N=5, F=2, instance (0,0), one command, owner as recoverer); the scenario was not repeated with a non-owner recoverer or with several commands in a batch.

The empty-command decision's execution-side effects are now read off the executor's own guards and loops with their anchors (epaxos/exec.go:24-30, 76-78, 122-134; epaxos/epaxos.go:398-423) rather than inferred loosely, but they are still not executed: no run drove the executor, so the ordering of dependents and any state-machine effect of a zero-length batch under a real run remain unexercised. The client-side effect is measured for this scenario, including the absence of a re-offer and the empty reply writer.

The decoding behaviour is stated for the PrepareReply decoder that this path uses, and the same run-time allocation is visible in a second decoder in the same file - PreAccept.Unmarshal allocates its command slice with make([]state.Command, alen1) at epaxos/defs.go:362-366, exactly as PrepareReply.Unmarshal does at 227-231 - so the shared pattern now rests on two inspected decoders rather than on the generated Marshal/Unmarshal shape alone; the remaining decoders in the file were not inspected.

The kept runs end with the instance at PREACCEPTED and the owner's command re-proposed rather than with an accepted value, and the losing runs end at PREACCEPTED with an empty batch; what a deciding quorum of the restarted phase 1 then does is outside this probe, which stops before any later round is driven.

Delivery order is measured with all six permutations of the three-reply set (2,4,3; 3,4,2; 3,2,4; 2,3,4; 4,2,3; 4,3,2) and four orders of the four-reply set (1,2,3,4; 1,3,4,2; 3,4,1,2; 3,1,4,2); the trigger position is observed directly (the delivery whose delivery replaces the bookkeeping object) rather than derived, and it is the same second reply in every recorded run.

The claim that no second dispatch can follow the trigger rests on the reply accounting (self reply plus peer replies equal N, of which SlowQuorumSize are consumed) together with the measured appended counts in the fresh bookkeeping; it is not a measured absence in a configuration with more replicas.
interpretations.joint_history: The four receipts cited here belong to the same probe construction and the same configuration (N=5, F=2, instance (0,0), one command, owner as recoverer), and each index is read inside its own receipt: 81a44ff62122417db3cc5697fc5303f6 index 0 the owner's pre-recovery state, index 3 the empty acceptor, index 4 the bookkeeping after the recovery replies, index 5 the first run's outcome and indices 9-11 the same for its second run; 098ab4425325464192aa558be557f0ce indices 0 and 2-4 the client-facing run whose decided instance holds an empty command list; e89ecb076e8d4a78b174f848562ed77f indices 6, 13 and 20 the three delivery orders of the three-reply set; and 251562364ca64b3c80cd14e0d6aeddc3 indices 5, 15, 25 and 35 the observed trigger delivery of the four four-reply orders with indices 9, 19, 29 and 39 their outcomes. The newly bound experiment e25f403842234594881914f730efff4e-experiment is the revision that added the observed trigger and the four orders; it changes no handler and no scenario parameter used by the earlier receipts. The receipt 2ba5ed477d854a01adbca361e9a8a918 extends the same tie construction to the three remaining permutations; each index is read inside its own receipt (27, 34 and 41 are that receipt's run outcomes for the orders 2,3,4; 4,2,3 and 4,3,2).

inst.lb = r.newLeaderBookkeepingDefault()
	lb := inst.lb
	lb.clientProposals = proposals
	lb.ballot = inst.vbal
	lb.seq = inst.Seq
	lb.cmds = inst.Cmds
	lb.deps = inst.Deps
	lb.status = inst.Status
	r.makeBallot(replica, instance)

	inst.bal = lb.lastTriedBallot
	inst.vbal = lb.lastTriedBallot
	preply := &PrepareReply{
		r.Id,
		replica,
		instance,
		inst.bal,
		inst.vbal,
		inst.Status,
		inst.Cmds,
		inst.Seq,
		inst.Deps}

	lb.prepareReplies = append(lb.prepareReplies, preply)
	lb.leaderResponded = r.Id == replica

	r.bcastPrepare(replica, instance)
